decks.title: Methods: Header, Parameters, Return and Pass by Value
goals: Explain how methods support modular programming and write the prototype and signature of a method
Define and call void and value-returning methods, and use return correctly
Predict the output of programs in which a method changes a primitive parameter, and define pass by reference with one example

slides.heading: User-defined methods
slides.body_md: Part 1: why we write **methods**, the **header**, **prototype** and **signature**, **parameters**, **return** and **pass by value**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: why methods, the header, prototype and signature, parameters and return, and pass by value
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to user defined methods. In this part we see why programs are divided into methods, and we take a method header apart. We separate the prototype from the signature, and the actual parameters from the formal ones. We learn how return works and what can go wrong with it. Finally we study pass by value, using a swap method that does not work.

slides.heading: Why write methods?
slides.body_md: A **method** is a named block of statements that does one job. Dividing a program into methods is **modular programming**: each part can be written, tested and reused on its own.

rows: the same statements are typed again and again
test and correct one small method
change every copy of the code
change the method in one place
each method has a name that says what it does

visual.alt: Table comparing one long main method with a program split into methods: repeated work, finding an error, changing a rule and reading
visual.caption: Modular programming: one task, one method.

slides.narration: A method is a named block of statements that does one job. Dividing a program into small methods is called modular programming. Code written once can be called again and again, so it is not repeated. An error is easier to find in a small method than in a long main. A rule can be changed in one place. The table compares the two styles.

slides.heading: The method header

headers: In `public static double milkBill(int litres, double rate)`
rows: the method belongs to the class
kind of value sent back (void if none)
type and name of each formal parameter

visual.alt: Table of the five parts of a method header: access specifier public, modifier static, return type double, name milkBill and the parameter list of an int and a double
visual.caption: The body in braces follows the header.

slides.narration: The first line of a method is its header. It has an access specifier, such as public, and a modifier such as static. Next comes the return type, which is the kind of value sent back, or void if nothing is sent back. Then come the name of the method and, in brackets, the list of parameters, each with its type and name. The statements in braces form the body.

slides.heading: Prototype and signature
slides.body_md: The **prototype** is the return type, the name and the parameter list. The **signature** is only the **name and the types of the parameters, in order**. The return type is **not** part of the signature.

rows: `public static double milkBill(int litres, double rate)`

visual.alt: Table of three methods with their prototype, which has the return type, name and parameter list, and their signature, which has only the name and the parameter types
visual.caption: The return type is in the prototype but not in the signature.

slides.narration: The prototype of a method gives its return type, its name and its parameter list. The signature is smaller. It is the name and the types of the parameters in order. The return type is not part of the signature, and neither are the names of the parameters. This difference will matter when we study overloading, because the compiler tells methods apart by their signatures.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: define and call

rows: `return litres * rate;` works out the product
the value goes back and is stored in amount; the println joins it to the text

visual.alt: Trace of the milk bill: the call passes 12 and 56.5, the method returns 678.0 and the program prints Amount = 678.0

slides.narration: Let us trace the milk bill program. The call in main passes twelve and fifty six point five. The formal parameters litres and rate receive copies of these values. The return statement works out the product, six hundred seventy eight, and sends it back. The value is stored in the variable amount, and the println joins it to the text. The output is Amount equals six hundred seventy eight point zero.

slides.heading: Quick check: parts of a header
slides.body_md: Match each part of the header with its name.
slides.narration: Recall the five parts of a header, and say which of them is the access specifier, the modifier, the return type and the parameter list.

slides.heading: void and value-returning methods

visual.alt: Table contrasting a void method, called as a statement and printing Welcome, Meera, with a value-returning method, whose result is stored in a variable
visual.caption: A void method is called as a statement; a value-returning method is used where its value is needed.

slides.narration: A void method sends nothing back, so its call is a statement on its own. In the notice program, greet is called twice, and each call prints a welcome line. A value returning method is different. Its call is used where the value is needed, for example on the right of an assignment, as in the milk bill. The table shows both kinds side by side.

slides.heading: return ends the method

visual.alt: Trace table of the age band method: age 9 returns Child; age 15 returns Teen; age 41 returns Adult; the first return that is reached ends the method
visual.caption: return ends the method at once, so the later returns are skipped.

slides.narration: The return statement sends a value back and ends the method at once. A method can have several return statements in different branches. In the age band method, age nine takes the first return and gives Child. Age fifteen skips the first return, takes the second and gives Teen. Age forty one passes both tests and reaches the last return, which gives Adult.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: return types

visual.alt: Table of five methods with different return types: cube returns 27, half returns 3.5, isEven returns true, initial returns K and label returns No. 5

slides.narration: A method can return any type. The method cube returns an int, and for three the value is twenty seven. The method half divides by two point zero, so it returns a double, three point five for seven. The method is even returns a boolean, here true. The method initial returns a char, and label returns a String. The type in the header must match the value returned.

slides.heading: Quick check: signature
slides.body_md: Choose the signature of the method.
slides.narration: Remember what the signature includes and what it leaves out, in particular the return type and the names of the parameters.

slides.heading: When return goes wrong
slides.body_md: The compiler checks every path. A statement after `return` is **unreachable**; a value-returning method must **return on every path**; a `void` method may not return a value.

rows: a path with no return in a value-returning method
return with a value in a void method
storing a double result in an int variable
incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from double to int
method fare in class FareCalc cannot be applied to given types;
using the result of a void method
incompatible types: void cannot be converted to int

visual.alt: Table of six mistakes with methods and the real compiler messages: unreachable statement; missing return statement; incompatible types: unexpected return value; incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from double to int; method fare in class FareCalc cannot be applied to given types;; incompatible types: void cannot be converted to int

slides.narration: The compiler checks return statements carefully. A statement placed after a return can never run, so javac reports unreachable statement. If a method with a return type has a path that ends without a return, javac reports missing return statement. A void method cannot return a value, and the type of the returned value must fit the declared type. The table gives the real messages.

slides.heading: Actual and formal parameters
slides.body_md: **Actual parameters** are the values or variables in the **call**. **Formal parameters** are the variables in the **header**. They are matched by **position**; the number and types must fit.

visual.caption: Actual parameters supply the values; formal parameters receive them.

slides.narration: The values written in a call are the actual parameters. The variables written in the header are the formal parameters. When the call runs, each actual value is copied into the formal parameter in the same position. Here the values seven and twelve in main go into km and rate, and the method returns eighty four. The names may differ, but the number and types must agree.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the call and its parts

visual.alt: Table of the two calls of fare: with distance and perKm the method returns 84, with 3 and 15 it returns 45; the formal parameters are km and rate in both calls
visual.caption: Actual parameters may be variables or literals.

slides.narration: Look at the two calls of fare. In the first call the actual parameters are the variables distance and per km, and the method returns eighty four. In the second call the actual parameters are the literal values three and fifteen, and it returns forty five. In both calls the formal parameters are km and rate. Actual parameters may be variables, literals or expressions.

slides.heading: The life of a method call
slides.body_md: When the call is reached, **control passes to the method**; when the method ends, control returns to the call and the **returned value replaces the call**.

visual.alt: Flow of a method call: the call is reached, the actual values are copied to the formal parameters, the body runs, return sends the result back and the caller continues
visual.caption: The life of one method call.

slides.narration: This flow shows what happens during a call. The calling statement is reached. The values of the actual parameters are copied into the formal parameters. The body of the method runs. A return statement sends the result back, or the end of a void method is reached. Control then returns to the caller, which uses the value and moves to its next statement.

slides.heading: Quick check: order of a call
slides.body_md: Arrange the events of a method call.
slides.narration: Think about what must happen before the body can run, and what happens after the return.

slides.heading: Pass by value
slides.body_md: Java passes primitive arguments **by value**: the formal parameter is a **copy**. Whatever the method does to the copy never reaches the actual parameter.

visual.caption: Pass by value: the method works on copies.

slides.narration: Primitive arguments are passed by value. The formal parameter is a separate variable, which starts with a copy of the value. In the diagram, the variables x and y of main go into swap as the copies a and b. The method interchanges its copies, but x and y stay as they were. Nothing travels back from the copies, so the change is lost when the method ends.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: the swap that fails

visual.alt: Trace of the swap method with a equal 10 and b equal 20: `(start)` gives `10, 20 (t does not exist yet)`; `int t = a;` gives `10, 20, 10`; `a = b;` gives `20, 20, 10`; `b = t;` gives `20, 10, 10`
visual.caption: Inside the method the swap works; main never sees it.

slides.narration: Let us trace the swap method with ten and twenty. After the first statement, t holds ten. After the second, a holds twenty. After the third, b holds ten. So inside swap the values are interchanged, and the first line prints twenty ten. But main prints its own variables, which were never touched, so the second line prints ten twenty. To send a result back, a method must return it.

slides.heading: Pass by reference: definition and example
slides.body_md: In **pass by reference** the **reference** to the data is passed, so the formal and actual parameters refer to the **same data**. Passing an **object** is the usual example: a change to its data member is seen by the caller.

rows: a copy of the value (call by value)
the reference to the object (call by reference)
yes, a change to its data members

visual.alt: Table contrasting a primitive parameter, passed by value so that the caller sees no change and still prints Outside: 8000, with an object parameter, passed by reference so that the weight becomes 1700
visual.caption: Pass by reference needs only its definition and one example in the syllabus.

slides.narration: In pass by reference the reference to the data is passed, not a copy of a value. The formal parameter and the actual parameter then refer to the same data. The usual example is an object. In the dispatch program, the method adds packing to the weight of the parcel it receives, and main then shows seventeen hundred. A primitive parameter never behaves like this.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: small methods, each with one job; written once, reused
access specifier, modifier, return type, name, parameter list
prototype: return type, name, parameters; signature: name and parameter types only
sends a value back and ends the method; none after it; every path must return
actual in the call, formal in the header; matched by position and type
primitives are copied; the caller's variable is never changed

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: modular programming, the header, prototype and signature, return, parameters and pass by value

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Methods divide a program into small reusable parts. The header has the access specifier, modifier, return type, name and parameter list. The prototype includes the return type, the signature does not. Return ends a method, and every path of a value returning method must return. Actual parameters are in the call, formal parameters in the header. Primitive parameters are passed by value.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write a prototype with the return type, the name and **every parameter with its type**.
The signature has **no return type** and no parameter names: `area(int, int)`.
Check every path of a value-returning method for a `return`; nothing may follow a `return` in the same block.
To trace a call, copy the actual values into the formal parameters first, then run the body.
A method that changes a primitive parameter changes only its own copy: the caller's variable keeps its value.
slides.narration: Some exam tips. Write the prototype with the return type, the name, and every parameter with its type. The signature has no return type. Check that every path of a value returning method has a return, and that nothing follows a return. To trace a call, first copy the actual values into the formal parameters. A method that changes a primitive parameter changes only its own copy.

decks.title: Static and Non-static, Pure and Impure Methods, Overloading
goals: Distinguish static from non-static methods and call each correctly
Write a class with data members and several member methods invoked through an object
Classify a method as pure or impure with a reason
Write overloaded methods and identify the version called for a given argument list

slides.heading: static, pure and overloaded methods
slides.body_md: Part 2: **static** and **non-static** methods, calls through **objects**, **pure** and **impure** methods and **method overloading**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: static and non-static methods, calling each kind, pure and impure methods, overloading, promotion and ambiguity
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to the second part. We separate static methods from non static ones and learn to call each correctly, with the help of objects. Then we classify methods as pure or impure. Last, we study method overloading, in which several methods share one name, and we see how the compiler chooses between them, even when an argument has to be promoted.

slides.heading: static and non-static methods

rows: cannot use instance data members directly
can use the data members of its object

visual.alt: Table comparing a static method, which belongs to the class and needs no object, with a non-static method, which belongs to an object, uses its data members and is called through the object

slides.narration: A static method belongs to the class itself, so it needs no object. A non static method belongs to the objects, and it can use their data members directly. In the tuition class, centre is static and total is not. Total multiplies the data member fee by the months, so it must work on an object. The table lists the differences.

slides.heading: Calling each kind
slides.body_md: A static method is called by **name** inside its class, or as **ClassName.method()** from another class. A non-static method is called through an **object**: **object.method()**.

rows: `t.total(3)` with an object t of Tuition
a non-static method of the same class
`total(3)` works: the same object is used

visual.alt: Table of how each kind of method is called from main of the same class, from another class and from a non-static method of the same class
visual.caption: Rule: no object, no non-static call.

slides.narration: This table shows how each kind is called. A static method is called by its name inside the same class, or with the class name, a dot and the method name from another class. A non static method needs an object. First create the object with new, then write the object name, a dot and the method. Inside another non static method of the same class, the name alone works.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: static and non-static together

visual.alt: Trace of the tuition program: the static call prints Sunrise Tuition; after an object is created, t.total(3) prints 2700

slides.narration: Let us trace the tuition program. The first statement calls the static method centre by its name, and it prints Sunrise Tuition. Then an object is created with new, and nothing is printed. The last statement calls total through the object. The data member fee is nine hundred, and three months give two thousand seven hundred.

slides.heading: The static context errors
slides.body_md: The method `main` is static, so it runs without any object. It **cannot use a non-static method or data member by name**; it needs an object.

rows: `total(3)` written in static main, no object
non-static method total(int) cannot be referenced from a static context
non-static variable fee cannot be referenced from a static context
`t.centre()`: static method called through an object
compiles and works, but write Tuition.centre() to show it is static

visual.alt: Table of the static context mistakes with the real compiler messages: non-static method total(int) cannot be referenced from a static context; non-static variable fee cannot be referenced from a static context; and the legal but untidy call of a static method through an object
visual.caption: main is static, so it can reach non-static members only through an object.

slides.narration: The main method is static, so it runs before any object exists. It therefore cannot call a non static method by its name. The compiler says that the non static method cannot be referenced from a static context. The same message appears for a data member used inside a static method. The cure is to create an object. A static method can be called through an object, but it is better to use the class name.

slides.heading: Pure methods
slides.body_md: A **pure method** returns a result **without changing** the state of the object or anything else. It works from its arguments, and the same arguments always give the same result.

visual.alt: Table of a pure and an impure method: two calls of square(6) give 36 36 while two calls of issue(10) give 40 30, because issue changes the data member stock
visual.caption: Same arguments, same result: a mark of a pure method.

slides.narration: A pure method only works out a result and returns it. It changes no data member and nothing passed to it, so the same arguments always give the same result. In the table, two calls of square six give thirty six each time. The second method, issue, reduces the data member stock, so its two calls give forty and then thirty. That method is not pure.

slides.heading: Impure methods
slides.body_md: An **impure method** changes the state of the object, for example a **data member**, or the object passed to it. The same call can then give different results.

slides.narration: An impure method changes something: usually a data member of the object. In the kiosk program the price starts at twenty five, so cost of four gives one hundred. The void method revise sets the price to thirty. The same call, cost of four, now gives one hundred twenty. The result changed because revise changed the state of the object, so revise is the impure method.

slides.body_md: Classify each method and give a reason. The test is simple: **does the method change anything?**

visual.caption: Ask: does this method change anything? If yes, it is impure.

slides.narration: Let us classify four methods. Twice only works from its argument, so it is pure. Reset sets the data member count to zero, so it changes the state and is impure. Avg only computes from its two arguments, so it is pure. Stamp changes the weight of the parcel that was passed to it, so it is impure. The question to ask each time is whether the method changes anything.

slides.heading: Method overloading
slides.body_md: **Method overloading** means two or more methods with the **same name** in one class and **different parameter lists** (number, type or order). It is **compile-time polymorphism**.

rows: `int volume(int l, int b, int h)`

visual.alt: Table of the three overloaded volume methods: one int gives the cube version and prints 64, three ints give the cuboid version and print 30, two doubles give the cylinder version and print 628.0
visual.caption: Same name, different parameter lists.

slides.narration: In method overloading, several methods in one class share a name but have different parameter lists. They differ in the number, the type or the order of the parameters. Here volume has three versions. One int gives the cube. Three ints give the cuboid. Two doubles give the cylinder. The compiler chooses the version from the call, before the program runs, so overloading is compile time polymorphism.

slides.heading: What makes a valid overload
slides.body_md: The **signatures** must differ. A different **return type** or a different **parameter name** is not enough.

rows: `show(int a, double b)` and `show(double a, int b)`
different order of types (but a call such as show(2, 3) is ambiguous)

slides.narration: Two methods can be overloaded only if their signatures differ. A different number of parameters is enough. A different type is enough. A different order of types is also enough. But a different return type alone is not, and neither is a different name for the same parameter. In those cases the compiler says that the method is already defined in the class.

slides.narration: Let us find the version for each call. Show of seven is an exact match for the int version. Show of seven point zero matches the double version. The char A has no version of its own, so it is promoted to int, and the int version prints sixty five. The long value seven has no version either, so it is widened to double, and the double version prints seven point zero.

slides.heading: Type promotion in a call
slides.body_md: If there is **no exact match**, Java widens the arguments along **byte, short, int, long, float, double** (and **char to int**) and picks the nearest version.

visual.alt: Chain of widening conversions used when an exact version is missing: byte to short to int to long to float to double, and char also widens to int
visual.caption: Widening order (char goes to int).

slides.narration: When no version matches the argument types exactly, the compiler widens the arguments. The order of widening is byte, short, int, long, float and double, and a char widens to int. The nearest version that can accept the widened value is used. Narrowing never happens by itself, so a double argument can never go to a version that needs an int.

slides.narration: For each call, decide whether there is an exact version, and if not, which widening gives the nearest one.

slides.heading: Ambiguous calls
slides.body_md: If **two versions fit equally well**, the call is **ambiguous** and does not compile. Make one argument exact.

slides.narration: Sometimes two versions fit equally badly. The class has mix of int and double, and mix of double and int. The call with two and three needs one widening in either version, so neither is better, and the compiler reports that the reference is ambiguous. A call with two and three point zero is an exact match for the first version, so it compiles.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing the return type in the signature, or the parameter names in it.
- A value-returning method with a path that has no `return`, or a statement after `return`.
- Expecting a method to change the caller's `int` variable (a swap method, a raise method): only the copy changes.
- Calling a non-static method from `main` without an object.
- Overloading by changing only the return type or only the parameter name.
- Forgetting that `char` is promoted to `int`, and `int` to `double`, when choosing an overloaded version.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Prototype and signature questions: return type, name and every parameter with its type.
- Output questions: each line in the exact order and format.
- Error questions: the error named and the line given.
- Programs (15 marks): class and method structure, correct headers and returns, calls with right arguments, input and output, variable description or comments.

questions.solution_md: One mark for the prototype and the signature of the example, and one mark for the reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
The **prototype** of a method gives its return type, name and parameter list: `double area(double r)`. The **signature** has only the name and the parameter types in order: `area(double)`.

The difference matters because the compiler tells overloaded methods apart by their signatures; two methods with the same signature cannot be in one class, even if their return types differ.
